headlines.title: Air quality authorities order South Bay landfill to reduce odors
headlines.description: The Bay Area Air District has ordered operators of a San Jose waste management facility to correct air quality issues and reduce odors. The Newby Island Resource Recovery Park, located in north San Jose, is a landfill and recycling center bound by Interstate 880 to the east and the waterfront Alviso neighborhood to the west. It is operated by Phoenix-based company Republic Services Inc. through its subsidiaries International Disposal Corp. of California, which oversees the landfill, and Browning-Ferris Industries of California Inc., which runs the recycling center. According to the order, issued Wednesday by the Hearing Board of the Bay Area Air District, the facility is responsible for hazardous gas emissions over the years, prompting odor complaints from neighborhoods in San Jose, Milpitas, Fremont, and Newark. The Bay Area Air District is the agency responsible for protecting the air quality in the region. The Hearing Board is a five-member body within the air district that can issue abatement orders to pollution-causing entities, in this case, the operators of the Newby Island Resource Recovery Park. A 2024 study by the air district found that the Newby Island facility was the major source of the odors that residents were complaining about. Hydrogen sulfide, a gas linked to headaches, nausea, and asthma, was the primary pollutant causing the odors, a news release from the district said. In December 2025, the district ordered the operators of the facility to install continuous emission monitors to track hydrogen sulfide, after an investigation revealed that they were underreporting pollution concentrations. Wednesday’s abatement order reiterates the need for continuous emission monitors and directs the operators to improve landfill inspections using drones to better detect methane leaks. Another requirement outlined in the order is to automate the landfill gas collection system and to install air pollution monitors along the perimeter of the facility. “Families in the South Bay have lived with persistent odors and uncertainty about what is in the air near their homes,” said Philip Fine, executive officer of the Bay Area Air District, in the news release. “This order establishes enforceable deadlines, stronger monitoring and clear consequences if Newby Island fails to comply.” Failure to comply with the abatement order will lead to further enforcement, and the district will separately assess fines for the violations that led to this abatement order. A spokesperson for the International Disposal Corp. of California said that the firm appreciates the air district and the Hearing Board’s focus on increasing transparency around air quality concerns and will comply with the order. “IDCC will continue working constructively with regulators, residents and local stakeholders to meet those requirements,” said spokesperson Yessica del Rincon in an email. “IDCC and the Newby Island Landfill provide an essential service to our customers and remain committed to operating the facility safely and reliably.” Previously, in 2022, International Disposal Corp. of California and Browning-Ferris Industries of California Inc. agreed to pay $210,000 to settle with the district over 30 notices of violation from 2014 to 2020 for non-compliance with air quality regulations at the landfill. The violations included landfill gas surface leaks associated with composting operations in 2014 and 2015, landfill wellhead positive pressure violations between 2015 and 2019, and gas collection shutdowns in 2019. The settlement also cited public nuisance violations based on odor complaints between 2014 and 2016.

headlines.title: How to watch San Jose State vs. USC in season opener on NBC and Peacock
headlines.description: Two California college football teams are getting ready for kickoff, as No. 14 USC will host San Jose State in a season-opening matchup. Lincoln Riley is entering his fourth year at the helm for USC after leading the team to a 9-4 record in 2025. Quarterback Jayden Maiava is back as a redshirt senior after leading the Big Ten in total offense a season ago, while leading rushers King Miller and Waymond Jordan are also returning to the Trojans. San Jose State is coming off a 3-9 season with Hawai’i transfer Luke Weaver expected to fill the void left at quarterback by Walker Eget, who transferred to Duke. Can USC get off on the right foot, or will San Jose State start the season with a stunning upset? Here’s what to know for the matchup and how to watch on NBC and Peacock: College Football Aug 24 College Football Aug 17 When is the San Jose State vs. USC game? headlines.title: 2 wildfires burn along California's scenic Big Sur coast
headlines.description: Fire crews with water-dropping aircraft attacked a small wildfire that prompted new evacuations Thursday along California’s remote Big Sur coast, where a much larger blaze has been burning for nearly three weeks. The Plaskett Fire erupted the previous day in steep terrain in Monterey County near Highway 1. Officials briefly closed a portion of the scenic coastal route Thursday afternoon as firefighters scrambled to keep the flames from running through canyons. A handful of isolated properties were under evacuation orders and warnings. The fire had no containment so far, and its cause was under investigation. About 40 miles (60 kilometers) to the north, officials closed another section of the highway where the Timber Fire has been active since Aug. 8. Crews performed back-burning operations, deliberately setting fire to brush to keep the bigger blaze from advancing toward populated areas of Big Sur. The larger fire was nearly 31 square miles (80 square kilometers), with more than 20% containment. Fire danger is high in much of California due to an increased risk of lightning and gusty winds from the remnants of a tropical storm in the Pacific.

headlines.title: Oakland's Laney College honors legendary coach John Beam as new football season kicks off
headlines.description: Oakland’s Laney College honored slain football coach John Beam Thursday as the team kicked off a new season. Players sported “JB” stickers on their helmets in honor of the legendary coach, who was shot and killed at Laney College’s field house last November. His death rocked the community and the thousands of current and former players whose lives he influenced. “This is the first time that we’re back on the field, all here really in the house that John built,” interim Laney College President Becky Opsata said. “We’re just happy to be back – a new fall at Laney College all working together for our students and community.” The college plans to open a new field house later this year that will be named after Beam. headlines.title: Small items get second life at San Francisco's ‘Strange Exchange'
headlines.description: It’s Tuesday morning and Lela Means is in her San Francisco garage, unpacking, weighing, and sorting thousands of small items – sunglasses, pieces of fabric, and picture-hanging wire, to name just a few. It’s the kind of stuff a person typically keeps in a junk drawer. To Means, however, it’s not “junk.” They are small, useful items simply in need of a new home. To understand why Means is doing all this, you have to go back several years and several thousand miles away to a different garage in Pennsylvania. After her mother died, Means was sorting through the belongings at her home. The larger items went to Goodwill. Trash went into the garbage. But many possessions didn’t fit neatly into either category. “I’d say they were too good for the landfill and maybe too small for Goodwill,” Means said. “Things like sunglass cases, broken jewelry, partially used craft supplies and pieces of fabric.” Rather than throw those items away, Means boxed them up and brought them back to San Francisco. There, she and a friend came up with an idea. What if they set up a table at a local farmers’ market and offered those small but useful items to anyone who wanted them? What if they invited others to do the same? The result was a community swap table they called “Strange Exchange“. “A lot of people go, ‘Why are you doing this?'” Means said. “And we usually answer, ‘Because it’s fun.’ We enjoy knowing that this stuff is finding a new home.” Means doesn’t describe the concept as recycling. Instead, she calls it “reshuffling” – helping items move from one person who no longer needs them to someone who does. When “Strange Exchange” launched, she had no idea how people would respond. Three years later, she has her answer. The high number of regular customers lets her know the people love it. So does she. “We just love interacting with other people in our community and meeting people who might have ideas about new stuff we can collect.” Most Sunday mornings, “Strange Exchange” can be found at the Divisadero Farmers’ Market, set up in the parking lot next to the local DMV. Visitors browse through an ever-changing assortment of items and often leave behind things they no longer need. At first, Means thought that if the project proved successful, she might expand it to multiple farmers’ markets. Over time, however, she realized she was happiest focusing on a single location and making it the best it could be. She’s not trying to change the world. She simply wants to improve her corner of it. She hopes others are inspired to do the same. “That’s what’s so great about ‘Strange Exchange,'” Means said. “Anyone can do this. You can do it at a school, at an office, anywhere. You don’t need to buy everything new.” For Means, that’s the real value of the project: creating a simple, community-driven way to reduce waste, share resources and make sure useful items find their next home.

headlines.title: Milpitas father among those missing after catastrophic floods in Nepal-Tibet border
headlines.description: A Milpitas man is among those missing following the catastrophic floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border. Floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border have buried homes, swept away roads and left entire communities under debris. More than 1,000 people were reported missing; among them was 48-year-old Prabhath Sajeepa, a U.S. citizen who lives in Milpitas. His brother says Sajeepa, originally from India, has been an American citizen for about 15 years. He is also a father of two, and was among the, at least, 77 people on a pilgrimage organized by the Isha Foundation. “They were returning back on the 26th and they were checking into a Nepal Immigration Center, and this is what happened. That’s what we know. We were not able to connect with him afterwards,” Sajeepa’s brother Praneeth Kumar said. His family says Sajeepa was near one of the buildings hit by the flood when communication stopped. Nepali authorities are now identifying Americans who remain unaccounted for, including a north Texas couple who traveled to the region on a religious journey. In the Bay Area, a community with deep ties to Nepal felt the impact. “There are yet a lot of people who are still undiscovered, and we are just praying and hoping they are safe,” Nepali Association of Northern California President Preteesh Karki said. Rescuers are still picking through mud and debris looking for any sign of life. For Sajeepa’s family, every minute brings more uncertainty. The videos from the disaster are too painful to watch, but they are still holding on to hope. That hope is also bringing the Bay Area’s Nepali community together. A candlelight vigil is planned for Friday at 7 p.m. at the Nepali Community Center in Richmond to honor those killed and stand with the families still waiting for answers.

headlines.title: Gwen Stefani, Usher to headline Dreamfest at Oracle Park
headlines.description: Gwen Stefani and Usher are heading to San Francisco next month to headline Dreamfest 2026. The concert is set to take over Oracle Park on Sept. 16 as the official celebration of Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference. Dreamfest also doubles as UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospitals’ Concert for Kids, which raises money to support pediatric care. The concert will follow an awards ceremony where a UCSF patient will be honored with the Colin Powell Medal of Courage. Admission to Dreamfest is included with eligible in-person Dreamforce registration. Separate benefit tickets and sponsorship packages are also available, starting at $1,500.

headlines.title: ICE arrests surge in Bay Area. Most appear to have no convictions or pending charges
headlines.description: ICE arrests soared to new highs across the country in July, with the surge in the Bay Area largely driven by the apprehension of immigrants with no known criminal convictions or pending charges, according to newly released ICE data obtained through a FOIA lawsuit by the Deportation Data Project. ICE documented roughly 49,000 arrests in July, the highest monthly total of President Trump’s second term, according to an NBC Bay Area analysis of the data. The data now includes the city where ICE recorded each arrest. In Bay Area cities, according to the data, the agency reported more than 330 arrests in July, a 76% jump from the same month last year. More than half of those arrests – about 189 – occurred in San Francisco. Immigration attorneys say they have seen many arrests occurring out of the public eye, including at ICE check-ins and immigration appointments. “That has been the trend in the Bay Area for the most part,” said Milli Atkinson, Director of the Immigrant Legal Defense Program for the San Francisco Bar Association. “People going voluntarily to their hearings, to their appointments, to their interview, and being detained at the 630 Sansome location in San Francisco or the location in Stockton.” Most of those arrested in San Francisco – about 83% – have no past criminal convictions or pending charges, according to the data. Atkinson said they’re seeing an uptick of arrests at airports and cautioned that anyone who is not a US citizen or lawful permanent resident could be a target. “Most of the arrests that we’ve seen at airports are people who at one point had a visa into the United States and that visa has expired,” Atkinson said. “But many of these people still have lawful presence in the United States. They have a work permit. They have an application pending.” ICE said it does not comment on the Deportation Data Project’s findings as it cannot “verify the source of, accuracy, completeness, or methodology of the data.” “The bottom line is that the Deportation Data Project is not accurate,” the agency said in a statement. The Deportation Data Project says on its website the records were produced by ICE in response to a FOIA lawsuit. ICE added that nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of “illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S.,” but did not provide supporting data or specify what time period it was referring to.

headlines.title: Teen arrested in connection with deadly mass shooting at party near Morgan Hill
headlines.description: A 17-year-old was arrested on Thursday in connection with a deadly shooting at an unsanctioned party near Morgan Hill, the Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office said. The sheriff’s office said the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody after authorities served a high-risk search warrant at a home in Salinas. He was arrested in connection with the mass shooting at an unsanctioned party in unincorporated Morgan Hill that left one person dead and injured six others on July 25, authorities said. More than 300 people were at the party, according to the sheriff’s office. Authorities said the suspect was identified after the community submitted numerous tips, videos and photos through the FBI’s digital media tip line. headlines.title: Overnight fire damages Concord market
headlines.description: Fire crews responded to an overnight fire at a market in Concord early Friday morning. The fire was reported at about 2:49 a.m. at Mas Primos Market, located at 1301 Galindo Street, according to information from PulsePoint. Crews had cleared the scene by shortly before 5:20 a.m. There was no immediate information about injuries or the extent of the damage. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

headlines.title: Pokémon madness takes over San Francisco for World Championships
headlines.description: Pokémon fans from around the world are descending on San Francisco this weekend for the Pokémon World Championships and the franchise’s first-ever fan convention. The three-day celebration is centered around Moscone Center, where thousands of fans and competitors are expected to gather. Organizers are transforming the area around the convention center into the world of Pokémon, complete with Bay Area landmarks such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Painted Ladies. Even Howard Street between Third and Fourth streets is getting a Pokémon makeover, becoming “Rayquaza Road” for the weekend. While the Pokémon World Championships are held annually, this year’s event includes a major first: Pokémon XP, an inaugural fan convention opening Friday morning. About 50,000 people are expected to attend the festivities, with roughly 2,500 players competing in the world championships. In addition to the events at Moscone Center, free Pokémon-themed activities will be held across San Francisco throughout the weekend. headlines.title: Caltrans spending $500,000 to remove eucalyptus trees in Montara
headlines.description: Crews have begun to clear stands of highly flammable eucalyptus trees from Caltrans land that homeowners in the San Mateo County town of Montara had pushed to remove ahead of this fire season. Using chainsaws and giant excavators and chippers, crews have started clearing across 15 acres of land Caltrans purchased decades ago to build a bypass around the treacherous Devil’s Slide area of Highway 1. Caltrans never used the land, and over time, it turned into strips of dense, flammable forests alongside the neighborhood. “I am really amazed and over the moon, I’m over the moon,” said Larry De Young, a retired biologist who led the fight to get Caltrans to act. He watched recently as crews made quick work of the smaller eucalyptus trees, using excavators to knock them down and to load the remains into chippers. “I think it’s incredibly improved,” he said. “They’re not finished yet, so I think it’s going to improve even more.” The most dramatic difference is where a stand of eucalyptus had towered over the backyards of homes, leaving only stumps and wood chips. “So right now we’re creating a 30 feet barrier around our right of way,” said Caltrans spokesman Pedro Quintana, adding that the agency has dedicated a half million dollars to double the originally planned firebreak on the advice of Cal Fire. The hope, he says, is that the effort will provide some relief to anxious homeowners. “They came to us and said, ‘hey, we have a concern.’ We heard their concerns… and we took action,” Quintana said. “This is a small piece,” said Christopher Hipkin, a veteran forester with Professional Tree Care in Berkeley, holding a strip of eucalyptus bark that he says can be deadly in a wildfire. “There’s huge pieces in here that could be burned off these trees and fly in a wind event for thousands of feet.” Crews are leaving some mature trees standing, he says, along with trees with active bird nests. Dozens of others are marked in red, designating that they be cut down to limit fire risk. “So basically, we’re putting this forest in a much more safe condition, reducing the hazards,” he said, adding that the work will last about another month. “Now, is that the end of the story? It isn’t because this forest is going to grow, these trees are going to throw seeds.” The only way to protect the community, he says, is develop a long-term strategy to control the threat but cutting down trees every few years. But De Young is just thankful for what’s been done by Caltrans so far with the stand of eucalyptus by his and his neighbors’ homes. “We’re talking about a very large, very rich state agency that was opposing us — and to have this happen within 14 months of us starting the battle is incredible.”
